Conversation content on Day 52: [|User|]: Read the passage below and answer the question or follow the instruction: Can you summarize the impact of infield shifts on preventing hits in baseball games according to the data provided by Inside Edge?

Passage: When Nate Eovaldi lost a no-hitter in the seventh inning Monday night on a single through the vacated left side of the infield, YES broadcaster David Cone said what a lot of Yankee fans were surely thinking.
Cone didn't seem to be passing judgment so much as stating a fact that's obvious to anyone who watches baseball these days: infield overshifts are as much a part of the modern game as walk-up music for hitters.
And moments like Eovaldi losing a no-no on a once-easy ground-out raise questions about whether shifting is overdone at times. However, Yankees GM Brian Cashman scoffs at such skepticism.
In fact, he likens not shifting to playing a crazy hunch at the blackjack table.
"It'd be like sitting next to the guy who's hitting on 19,'' Cashman said by phone. "You'd be like, 'dude, what are you doing?' "
Yes, the GM believes strongly in the data that his analytical department provides him as a basis for decisions on shifting. The Yankees were one of the early proponents of shifting, but now even teams that aren't so sabermetrically-inclined have joined the party.
But to what extent? And how effective are shifts, in general and as they apply to specific teams, even individual pitchers?
Inside Edge, an analytics company that some major league teams pay for data on which they base shifting decisions, provided the Daily News with answers to those questions.
And while the overall number of shifts is rather staggering these days, the surprise is how few plays they actually affect.
In 289 games played around the majors through Monday, teams used a total of 4,032 shifts. With those shifts employed, the ball was put in play 3,103 times, or 71.1 percent of the time.
The scoreboard, according to Inside Edge?
Shifts prevented hits 218 times. They aided hits 163 times. They weren't a factor 2,721 times.
So what's the big deal? Well, considering that only about an eighth of the season has been played, and shifts have already prevented 55 more hits than they have aided, that's a pace to prevent some 440 hits, divided by 30 teams.
Of course, some teams shift more often than others. And some benefit more than others. The most fascinating overall statistic is that the team that shifts the most, the Astros, who have done so 46 percent of the time, have the worst prevent/aid percentage in the majors: their shifts had prevented eight hits, while aiding 15.
As for the local teams, they are a contrast in styles, the Yankees shifting much more than the Mets, and with more success this season, according to Inside Edge.
Through 18 games, the Mets had shifted only 55 times, an 11 percent shift rate that was the second-lowest among all teams. Only the Marlins, at 7 percent, had shifted less.
Shifting isn't helping the Mets so far either. According to the Inside Edge numbers, they are one of the five teams whose shifts have aided more hits than they've prevented — by a count of 4-2.
Meanwhile, the Yankees had shifted 180 times through 17 games, the fifth-highest percentage among all teams. Of those 180 shifts, Inside Edge says 12 of them prevented hits, while eight of them aided hits, including the one by Rangers' rookie Nomar Mazara that broke up Eovaldi's no-hitter. It should be noted that Eovaldi has not been benefited by the shift at all this season, including during Monday night's no-no bid.
Cashman might object to those numbers. His analytics department does their own tracking and evaluating of the shifts, and while he won't reveal specifics, he makes them sound impressive.
It's true, you tend to forget the many balls up the middle that once would have been hits are now turned into outs by the shift, but the one area I question pertains to the hit against Eovaldi.
That is, does extreme velocity change the equation? Specifically, aren't the odds pretty good that a lefty hitter, in this case the rookie Mazara who has little track record on which to base a shift, is going to hit Eovaldi's 95-mph fastball on the outside corner to the opposite field?
Cashman insisted that every variable is accounted for in the Yankees' data, and said high velocity rarely changes hitters' tendencies.
Nevertheless, Inside Edge also provided shift numbers for each of the Mets' and Yankees' pitchers, and two of the four the shift has hurt more than helped this season are Eovaldi and Noah Syndergaard, because they've given up opposite-field ground ball singles on fastballs 95 mph or higher.
SHOULD MORE SPRING TRAINING GAMES BE PLAYED AT NIGHT?
Most pitchers, at heart, aren't fans of shifting anyway, as former Met and Yankee Al Leiter, now an MLB Network analyst, explains.
The one active pitcher who has complained publicly is Clayton Kershaw, who might be the best in the game. Late in spring training he voiced his opinion to reporters, essentially reaffirming Leiter's point, that watching a soft ground ball become a hit because of the shift is hard to take.
All indications are Kershaw is still having that type of influence. Under GM Andrew Friedman the Dodgers are considered one of the most sabermetrically-influenced organizations in baseball, yet they've shifted only 16 percent of the time, the 10th-lowest in the majors.
They're also one of the five teams whose shifts have aided more hits than they've prevented.
In any case, Kershaw seems to be the rare exception, a player whose status and strong sentiment influences a team's philosophy and the general trend toward more shifting.
Some baseball people make a case for the overall trend changing in years to come, noting that organizations are prioritizing contact hitting in the minors and teaching hitters to use the entire field, a practice that could eventually reduce shifting.
But clearly shifting in some form here is to stay, though not to everyone's liking, including Joe Girardi. On Tuesday, the day after a shift cost Eovaldi his no-hitter, the Yankee manager said if it was his choice he'd ban shifting from baseball, saying he thinks the game should be played as it has been for decades.
However, Girardi also made a point of saying he's going to use the rules to his advantage, and continue shifting. Not that he'd really have any choice. Shifting in baseball is dictated by data-driven front offices, not the manager.
And there aren't many GMs who, as Cashman would put it, hit on 19 when they sit at the blackjack table.
[|AI|]: According to data provided by Inside Edge, infield shifts are effective in preventing hits in baseball games. In 289 games played around the majors, teams used a total of 4,032 shifts, and the ball was put in play 3,103 times or 71.1% of the time. Shifts prevented hits 218 times and aided hits 163 times. However, the study also found that some teams benefit more from shifting than others, and that even teams that shift the most, such as the Astros, have the worst prevent/aid percentage in the majors. The Yankees shift much more than the Mets, and with more success this season. The Mets are one of the five teams whose shifts have aided more hits than they've prevented, while the Yankees have had shifts that prevented 12 hits and aided eight, including one hit that broke up a no-hitter. While some baseball people predict the overall trend changing in years to come as organizations start prioritizing contact hitting and teaching hitters to use the entire field, shifting in baseball is currently dictated by data-driven front offices, not the manager.
